analysis.one_liner: Requires lead-paint hazard testing before young children move into federally assisted older housing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was sent to the House Financial Services Committee in June 2018 and stayed there until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required owners of federally assisted housing built before 1978 to test for lead-paint hazards before a family with a child under six moves in, and to fix any hazards within 30 days. A visual inspection alone wouldn't count. If hazards weren't fixed, the family could move immediately to a lead-safe unit with no waitlist, no penalty, and no gap in housing assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children living in or moving into federally assisted housing built before 1978, the housing stock where lead paint exposure is most common. Children under six are the group most harmed by lead exposure, which causes permanent developmental damage. Neighbors and building residents also benefit from required notices when hazards are found.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Young children in federally assisted older housing

how_it_helps.text: HUD must write rules requiring a lead-hazard risk assessment before a family with a child under six occupies covered housing, with assessments within 15 days for housing using Section 8 vouchers, public housing, or project-based rental assistance [S2][S3].
A visual inspection would no longer count as enough; owners must fix identified hazards within 30 days, with no extensions, and notify all affected residents [S2][S3].
A family in a unit with uncontrolled lead hazards could relocate on an emergency basis to a lead-safe or post-1978 unit without a waitlist, penalty, or lapse in assistance [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of pre-1978 federally assisted housing, who would bear the cost of risk assessments, lead-hazard control work within 30 days, and emergency relocations. The bill authorized federal appropriations for fiscal years 2019 through 2023 to carry out the program, so taxpayers could also share the cost [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Owners of pre-1978 federally assisted housing

drawbacks.text: The testing and 30-day remediation requirements fall on owners of older federally assisted housing, including small landlords, and could discourage some from participating in federal housing programs or add costs passed through rents [S2].
The bill was an authorization of appropriations with no dedicated funding source, so the actual cost to taxpayers and to HUD administration was left open [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are one-sided: lead exposure causes permanent harm to young children, and the bill targeted exactly the older, federally supported housing where that exposure happens. The main cost is remediation spending by owners, which is the point of the policy; the open-ended funding authorization was a real but ordinary drafting gap.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald McEachin introduced the bill on June 27, 2018, joined by Republican Rep. John Faso as an original cosponsor [S1][S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, which was the only committee action the bill ever received [S5].
The bill attracted 9 cosponsors, 8 Democrats and 1 Republican, but never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of pre-1978 federally assisted housing are better off because the bill died: they never faced the new testing, 30-day remediation, and relocation requirements, and HUD was never required to write the rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Owners of older federally assisted housing

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor, a Republican original cosponsor, and 8 Democrats plus 1 Republican among the 9 cosponsors — but no vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: Owners and landlords of pre-1978 federally assisted housing
industries.note: The bill would have required paid risk assessments, 30-day hazard control, and emergency relocations in their units. The bill's death lets those costs — which are the price of removing lead hazards from children's homes — stay off their books.

industries.industry: Lead inspection, risk assessment, and abatement contractors
industries.note: Mandatory pre-occupancy risk assessments and clearance work would have created steady demand for licensed lead inspectors and remediation firms. With no law, that work remains voluntary in most cases.
